Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Celeste Poulin. I am the Division Director of
Quality Assurance and Regulation (QAR) within the Bureau of Agriculture, Food and Rural
Resources. I am speaking on behalf of the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry (DACF) as neither for nor against LD 1198, Resolve, Directing the Department ofAgriculture,
Conservation and Forestry to Assess Its Current Meat and Poultry Inspection Programs.

The Division of Quality Assurance and Regulation (OAR) is tasked with implementing state and federal laws regarding meat and poultry inspection in Maine. Our Meat and Poultry Consumer
Protection Inspectors are tasked with enforcing compliance with United States Department of
Agriculture (USDA) regulations regarding the slaughter, processing, and sale of meat and poultry
products to consumers. This includes maintaining "at least equal" status in relation to USDA
regulations. This means, in practice, that Maine must uphold the federal standards and requirements at
the very least and may be more restrictive but not less.
The proposed bill directs DACF to assess the Maine Meat and Poultry Inspection program and report findings to the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry Committee. We
note that the program regularly undergoes evaluation, including these examples:
0 The USDA Food Safety Inspection Service (FSIS) conducts an annual paper audit in
coordination with the offices of the USDA-F SIS Laboratory Quality Assurance, Response and Coordination (LQARCS), USDA-FSIS Office of the Chief Financial Officer (OCFO), and
USDA-FSIS Civil Rights Staff, Office of the Administrator (OA). We submit records,

10041198:
Joe Gray AUBURN LD 1198
I am writing today in support of LD 1198 a resolve directing the DACF to assess its current meat and poultry inspection programs. I wish it were a directive instructing them to overhaul their programs completely to eliminate all the unnecessary red tape that is crippling the small-scale meat processors in this state.
In the past inspectors and the DACF worked with producers and small-scale processors to increase availability of slaughtering dates. When Henrietta Boufet and her crew were in power they worked with folks to get more processors involved. They knew driving animals long distances to slaughter is not humane. They cared about animal welfare and the welfare of farmers and processors here in Maine.
In the past few years there has been nothing but conflict coming from DACF's Meat and Poultry Inspection Program. Even processors who have been licensed with DACF are switching to USDA inspections because there is less hassle.
We need MORE processors in this state. We need an easily understood program without all the hoops to jump through. It is difficult to even comprehend all the rules and regulations that are in place currently. Consequently, inspectors are free to punish at will. Instead of working with farmers and small-scale processors to address shortfalls or fix small issues, the state has chosen to be adversarial and punish at any and all opportunities.
Please vote for this resolve. It is a VERY small first step toward making the DACF responsive and responsible.

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry:
My name is Russ Black; and I represent Senate District 5, which is home to many agricultural producers. I'm here today to present LD ll98, "Resolve, Directing the Department of
Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry to Assess Its Current Meat and Poultry Inspection Programs."
This bill directs the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry to review the meat
and poultry inspection process and find ways to improve it for both producers and consumers. l've seen firsthand how difficult it can be for local farmers to navigate the current inspection system. Whether it's delays, confusion around exemptions, or complicated regulations, many
producers face real challenges trying to comply with the rules while keeping their businesses running smoothly.
This bill takes a thoughtful approach to addressing these issues. It will ask the Department to review the inspection process, including exemptions, and gather input from farmers, processors,
and experts like the University of Maine Cooperative Extension. By working with these groups, the Department can better understand the challenges and come up with solutions.
The bill also aims to give smaller producers more flexibility, which is important to help them
succeed. By reviewing the exemptions and working with federal agencies like the USDA, we can
make sure Maine's producers are held to the right standards without unnecessary red tape that can make it harder for them to thrive.
The Department will have until January 15, 2026, to submit a report with recommendations, and that will give us the chance to make any necessary changes. This bill is an important step toward improving the inspection process and supporting Maine's agricultural community.
I encourage the Committee to support this bill. Thank you for your time and consideration.

10041053:
kathy shaw Valley View Farm Auburn LD 1198
Good Afternoon Members of the DACF committee.
My name is Kathy Shaw, I am the owner of a small farm in Auburn Maine and am a former member of this committee..
I am writing today to offer my support for LD1198: A Resolve , Directing the Department of Agriculture , Conservation And Forestry to Assess Its Current Meat and Poultry Inspection Programs.
Regretfully , due to prior work commitments, I am unable to attend this hearing in person to offer testimony.
I urge this committee to move this resolve forward to help relieve the roadblocks in place for small producers that are looking to expand their farm offerings by the processing of local meats.
Over the past year, I have had conversations with Mr Lapine and Commissioner Amanda Beal regarding the confusing wording , endless "switchbacks"and difficulty in navigating the current wording for the meat and poultry inspection programs. I have listened in on lengthy conversations between my husband and other officials of the Department as he attempts to understand CLEARLY what is or is not allowed. We have poured over the documents provided from the state regarding rules and regulations that processors need to understand and comply with... and spent hours of our time , hours! Only to be more confused ...there should be a clearer way.
I operated a small local foods store in New Auburn for 5 years and when I initially opened the store had a congenial working relationship with the then inspector Marshall Piper. Mr Piper clearly explained the rules and regulations that we needed to comply with and was very willing to help us move forward and succeed...Now, I hear horrible stories almost every week about the inspectors , and their interpretations of the rules, their heavy-handed approach to producers and unwilling attitude to help our small producers become successful. And not long after Mr Piper retired, we "enjoyed " visits from inspectors that were aggressive, hostile and intimidating.
I am not sure when this shift occurred and why these rules and regulations are so confusing. I am positive that there is a better way forward, there should be a cleaner, easier set of regulations for producers to follow.
In a state that values the production of local foods , many small farmers are being forced to close shop or farm because it is difficult ( and farming takes an incredible leap of faith) to operate an agricultural operation in our state without running up against some type of rule, regulation or law that forbids poultry or meat production.
As a state, we owe it to our consumers and producers to be able to offer fresh locally produced foods for our good health and wellbeing. I have not met a farmer yet that intentionally and knowingly wants to harm their customers, neighbors and friends through tainted product. That does not make any type of good business sense. But the rules to comply should be clear, easy to read and interpret.
I thank you for your time today, and urge your support of this resolve.
Sincerely
Kathy Shaw Valley View Farm, Auburn Maine.
